clue.text: Priest suffers another hip dislocation

indicators.note: a dislocation puts things out of joint, so the letters of these two words are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: A clergyman has the misfortune of putting his hip out once again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suffers' is a link; 'dislocation' rearranges ANOTHER HIP. 'hip dislocation' reads as a medical phrase, hiding the split between fodder and indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: A hierophant was a chief priest of ancient Greek mysteries, an interpreter of sacred rites.

clue.text: Cheat gets nothing in such a set-up

indicators.note: in places the zero inside the rearranged letters
set-up suggests the letters are arranged afresh

parts.note: O is zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A swindler takes nothing from this kind of rigged arrangement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set-up' rearranges SUCH to HCUS; O goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: To hocus is to trick or hoax someone, as in hocus-pocus.

clue.text: Sense of well-being with British capital injected in this plant

indicators.note: injected in means inserted into, so the capital letter goes inside the word for elation

parts.note: euphoria is a feeling of elation

indicators.note: capital means the first, upper-case letter of the word

explanation.surface: Some British money pumped into a plant brings a feeling of well-being.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital' looks like money or London but means British's first letter, B.
explanation.definitionFit: Euphorbia is the spurge genus, a large group of flowering plants with milky sap.

clue.text: This outlaw might give you 'a handout, but never two

definitions.text: This outlaw might give you 'a handout, but never two

parts.words: This outlaw might give you 'a handout, but never two
parts.note: a slot machine with a single lever arm is pictured as a robber with one hand, so it can give a hand out but not two

explanation.surface: A bandit might offer charity, but only stingily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'handout' splits into 'hand out': a robber with one arm can only hold out one hand.
explanation.definitionFit: A fruit machine with a lever and a reputation for taking money is nicknamed this way.

clue.text: Crazy way perhaps to get in rent

indicators.note: to get in means entering, so the jumbled letters go inside the word for rent

parts.note: to rent is to hire

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters of the preceding word may be ordered differently

explanation.surface: A mad route may be the way to get your rent paid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges WAY to AYW; 'to get in' puts that inside HIRE.
explanation.definitionFit: Haywire means out of control or erratic, as of a person or machine gone wild.

clue.text: Feature John the. Poet in A Bunch of Flowers

parts.note: the nose is a facial feature
John Gay was the poet who wrote The Beggar's Opera

explanation.surface: A request to feature John the poet in an anthology titled after flowers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a link. 'A Bunch of Flowers' looks like a book title.
explanation.definitionFit: A nosegay is a small posy, a sweet-smelling bouquet.

clue.text: Poet said to be excluded

indicators.note: said tells us the word is spoken, so a word meaning excluded gives the sound of the entry

parts.note: to be excluded is to be barred

explanation.surface: A poet is apparently being kept out of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'said' makes BARRED sound like the written entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A bard is a traditional word for a poet, Shakespeare being the Bard.

clue.text: How congenial characters get from end to end

explanation.surface: How friendly people relate to each other all the way through.
explanation.walkthrough: Friendly people 'get along'; along also means lengthwise from one end to the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Compatible people get on, hence the phrase with this word; it also means lengthways through something.

clue.text: Note is struck as shown

parts.note: D is a musical note
taken as written
a note struck on an instrument is played

explanation.surface: A musical note is sounded as shown in the score.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Displayed means exhibited or put on view.

clue.text: As one of mankind, Pope's proper student?

definitions.text: As one of mankind, Pope's proper student?

parts.words: As one of mankind, Pope's proper student?
parts.note: Alexander Pope wrote that the proper study of mankind is man, so a scholar of humanity is his proper student

explanation.surface: A question about whether a human being is the ideal pupil of the Pope.
explanation.walkthrough: Pope is the poet Alexander Pope, not the pontiff; his Essay on Man says 'The proper study of mankind is man'.
explanation.definitionFit: This scientist studies human beings, their societies and cultures.

clue.text: Twopence coloured like this?

parts.note: plays on the old phrase 'penny plain, twopence coloured', while British pennies are bronze coins whose reddish metal colour is meant

explanation.surface: A question about the colouring of a cheap print or toy theatre sheet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penny plain, twopence coloured' described Victorian printed sheets sold plain or hand-coloured; here 'coloured' is taken literally, the shade of copper coins.
explanation.definitionFit: Copper-coloured means having the reddish-brown hue of the metal used in old pennies.

clue.text: "Gardens bright with — rills" (Coleridge)

parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Coleridge's poem Kubla Khan, where the missing adjective describes the winding streams

explanation.surface: A line from a Romantic poem with one word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The line from Kubla Khan runs 'And there were gardens bright with sinuous rills'.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word describes winding, curving streams, as a serpentine course twists and bends.

clue.text: About 100 therefore pressing for corporal punishment

indicators.note: about means going around, so the word for therefore wraps the Roman numeral

parts.note: therefore can mean so
C is the Roman numeral for 100
pressing means urging

explanation.surface: Someone is urging, around a hundred times over, for corporal punishment to return.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like 'approximately' with 100, but it tells SO to go round C, giving SCO.
explanation.definitionFit: Scourging is flogging with a whip, a severe bodily punishment.

clue.text: As a philosopher he, needs supporter's backing

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the word for a supporter is read in reverse

parts.note: a leg supports the body, so it is a supporter

explanation.surface: A thinker says he needs someone to back him up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' reverses LEG to GEL; 'As a' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Hegel was the German idealist thinker behind the dialectic, author of the Phenomenology of Spirit.

clue.text: Am I taking this message to be friendly?

definitions.text: Am I taking this message to be friendly?

parts.words: Am I taking this message to be friendly?
parts.note: the letters of AM I taking in a word for a message make a word meaning friendly, so the message is what joins AMI to form that friendly adjective

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether to read a message as a friendly one.
explanation.walkthrough: AMI + the answer gives AMICABLE, meaning friendly; 'message' is the definition, the rest says what joining it to AM I makes.
explanation.definitionFit: A telegram was commonly sent by wire, so the word for the wire came to mean the message itself.

clue.text: Usual trade on a railway

parts.note: custom means trade, as in a shop's business

explanation.surface: Business as normal on a train line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Customary means habitual or normal by tradition.

clue.text: A wordy, perhaps, yet gloomy science

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the following letters may be arranged in some other way

explanation.surface: A dismal-sounding discipline concerned with words.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges YET GLOOMY; 'A wordy' hints at the subject, the study of word origins.
explanation.definitionFit: Etymology is the study of how words originated and how their meanings developed, a branch of linguistic learning.

clue.text: Old tsarist comes from Portmadoc to Bristol

indicators.note: comes from signals the entry is found in the letters of the next words

explanation.surface: A Russian monarchist travels from a Welsh port to Bristol.
explanation.walkthrough: Portmadoc (now Porthmadog) is a Welsh harbour town; the run spans portmadOC TO BRISTol.
explanation.definitionFit: An Octobrist belonged to the Russian party that backed the Tsar's October Manifesto of 1905.

clue.text: Directors of the Royal. Observatory? Right

explanation.surface: A query about who runs the Royal Observatory, answered with approval.
explanation.walkthrough: Whimsically, astronomers' directors would be a board of stars; on a ship the right-hand side is starboard.
explanation.definitionFit: A board for stars would govern an observatory; and on a vessel the right side facing forward is starboard.

clue.text: What may make' one conspicuous, present company excepted

definitions.text: What may make' one conspicuous, present company excepted

parts.words: What may make' one conspicuous, present company excepted
parts.note: plays on being 'conspicuous by one's ...', and 'present company excepted' hints at not being there

explanation.surface: A polite aside about standing out in company.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'conspicuous by one's absence' means noticed because one is missing.
explanation.definitionFit: Absence is the state of being away, not present.

clue.text: Inscrutability, of Jas. Hook's ambition

explanation.surface: The impassive look that Captain Hook was after.
explanation.walkthrough: Captain James Hook's ambition in Peter Pan was to see Pan dead.
explanation.definitionFit: A deadpan expression shows no emotion; and Hook wished Peter Pan dead.

clue.text: Chose to work and do some haymaking

parts.note: OP is short for opus, a work
to ted is to spread out mown grass to dry

explanation.surface: Someone decided to get on with a job and help with the hay.
explanation.walkthrough: TED is a farming verb: to turn and spread new-mown hay.
explanation.definitionFit: Opted means selected or decided on one option.

clue.text: Vital part of church equipment

explanation.surface: An essential piece of what a church owns.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'of' is a link between two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: A bodily part such as the heart is a vital one; a church's pipe instrument is the other sense.

clue.text: A girl in distress sought by Arthur's knight

indicators.note: in distress suggests disorder, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A damsel in distress is rescued by a knight of the Round Table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A girl in distress' reads as the damsel of romance; 'in distress' rearranges A GIRL.
explanation.definitionFit: The Holy Grail was the sacred cup quested after by Arthurian knights such as Galahad.

clue.text: Listener caught by tearful type of pirate

indicators.note: caught by means held within, so the word for a weeper holds the hearing organ

parts.note: someone who sobs is a sobber
an ear is a listener

explanation.surface: Someone eavesdropping is seized by a pirate given to weeping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Listener' looks like a person but is the EAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A sea-robber is a plunderer of ships, another word for a buccaneer.

clue.text: The attack, we hear, spread out in all directions

indicators.note: we hear tells us the word for an attack is spoken, giving the sound of the entry

parts.note: an attack is a raid

explanation.surface: Reports say an assault fanned out everywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we hear' makes RAID sound like the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Rayed means radiating like beams from a centre.

clue.text: Such fabulous nights!.

parts.note: the fabulous nights are the tales of the Thousand and One Nights, told by Scheherazade

explanation.surface: An exclamation about some wonderful evenings out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fabulous' means full of fables, not just wonderful.
explanation.definitionFit: The collection of tales is known in English as the Arabian Nights.

clue.text: Contractual relationship -one in. Revised Version in Ruth

indicators.note: in places the preceding letters inside the word for compassion

parts.note: ruth is an old word for pity

indicators.note: in here places the numeral inside the abbreviation for the Bible translation

parts.note: RV is the abbreviation for the Revised Version of the Bible
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A legal relationship found in the Book of Ruth in the Revised Version.
explanation.walkthrough: Ruth looks like the Bible book but is the old noun for pity; I goes in RV to make RIV, which goes in PITY.
explanation.definitionFit: Privity is the legal relation between parties to a contract, allowing only them to enforce it.

clue.text: Loud cry heard in the Shetland Islands

explanation.surface: A shout echoes across the northern Scottish isles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heard' is a link, not a homophone sign; Yell is the second-largest island of Shetland, off northern Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: A shout or scream is a loud cry; Yell is also an island in that northern group.

clue.text: Form of control said to be put, back in place

parts.note: a rein is a strap for controlling a horse
said means stated

explanation.surface: A kind of control is declared to be restored.
explanation.walkthrough: 'said' here is a plain synonym, not a homophone sign.
explanation.definitionFit: Reinstated means restored to a former position or condition.
